cases.description: A reference to a record path that no file has resolves through a record alias, as aliased, with the alias's target, its fragment resolved in the record it moved to (§8.5, §13.6, decision C22).
A reference whose first step names no node of a record resolves through an anchor alias of that record, as aliased (§8.5, §13.6).
A reference that resolves only through an alias is a ref-aliased warning (§8.5, Appendix D).
For contrast, a record path and an anchor that exist resolve to the live nodes, although an alias has them as its old names (§13.6).

A live record path and a live anchor that an alias has as its old name are each an alias-shadowed warning, at the record and at the node, once for a node whose explicit and derived anchors both have the name (§13.6, Appendix D).

This case pins the project owner's answer on card AC: a live name shadows an alias whatever a link's first step reaches by it, a top-level key of a JSON or YAML record included, as it stops a chain of anchor aliases. The alias a to b in data/keys.json and data/keys.yaml is an alias-shadowed warning at the key a. For contrast, the alias n to b, whose old name is only a nested key that no first step reaches, and the alias gone to b, whose old name nothing has, raise nothing (§13.6, Appendix D).
For contrast, a record that no alias names raises nothing (§13.6).

In a journal whose root's sections are declared multimap, a first step that names no node of the record is not ambiguous, so the link done is dangling in the live store and resolves through the anchor alias done to finished, as aliased; tpyo, which no alias names, stays dangling; and monday, which names two sections, is ambiguous (§7.4, §8.5, §13.6, decision AP).
The same links in check: a ref-aliased warning, a ref-dangling error and a ref-ambiguous error, all at the $body that holds them (§8.5, Appendix D, decision AP).
